assessment_summary: The statement incorrectly asserts that depth-first search (DFS) finds the shortest-path distance, which is a property of breadth-first search (BFS). A simple triangle graph demonstrates that DFS can take a longer path and discover a vertex at a depth greater than its shortest-path distance.
counterexample: Consider an undirected, unweighted, connected graph with vertices {s, a, b} and edges {s,a}, {a,b}, {s,b}. Let the start vertex be s. The shortest-path distance from s to b is 1 (via edge {s,b}). If the depth-first search (DFS) explores the neighbours of s in the order [a, b], it will first visit a, adding it to the DFS tree at depth 1. From a, the next unvisited neighbour is b, so DFS visits b from a, adding b to the DFS tree at depth 2. Thus, the depth at which DFS discovers vertex b is 2, which does not equal its shortest-path distance of 1.
